content:
The [Standard Deviation Calculator](/standard-deviation-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Sample and population standard deviation and variance. Enter your data set (comma or space separated) and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Standard deviation measures how spread out values are from the mean. A small SD means values cluster tightly; a large SD means they're widely scattered. This guide explains how to use it, the formula it applies, and a worked example you can follow with your own numbers. Related Math tools include [Percentage Calculator](/percentage-calculator), [Fraction Calculator](/fraction-calculator) and [Square Root Calculator](/square-root-calculator). People also look for this tool as "variance calculator", "sample standard deviation", "population standard deviation".

## How to use the Standard Deviation Calculator

Start by typing or pasting your data set (comma or space separated). The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause. When you want a clean slate, Reset restores the defaults. The steps below walk through each input in order.

1. Type or paste your data set (comma or space separated).
2. Check the result — it updates instantly as you type.
3. Use Reset to start over with the default values.

## Formula

σ = √(Σ(x − μ)² ÷ N) for a population; s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)) for a sample.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Standard Deviation Calculator](/standard-deviation-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic. If the figures look wrong, check your inputs first — a misplaced decimal point is the usual culprit.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. For 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 the mean is 5 and the population SD is exactly 2. Try the same figures in the [Standard Deviation Calculator](/standard-deviation-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves. The steps are the same whatever numbers you use; only the figures change.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Data set (comma or space separated): 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9), the [Standard Deviation Calculator](/standard-deviation-calculator) returns Sample standard deviation (s): 2.13809, Population standard deviation (σ): 2, Sample variance: 4.571429, Mean: 5. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. Change any value and every figure updates instantly. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Percentage Calculator](/percentage-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Use sample SD when your data is a subset of a larger group.
- About 68% of normal data falls within 1 SD of the mean.

Keep these in mind and the figures will be as useful as the numbers you put in.

## Frequently asked questions

### Why divide by n − 1 for samples?

Bessel's correction removes bias when estimating population spread from a sample. Try it with your own numbers in the [Standard Deviation Calculator](/standard-deviation-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Variance vs standard deviation?

Variance is the SD squared; SD is in the same units as the data. Try it with your own numbers in the [Standard Deviation Calculator](/standard-deviation-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What formula does the Standard Deviation Calculator use?

σ = √(Σ(x − μ)² ÷ N) for a population; s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)) for a sample. You can see it in action in the [Standard Deviation Calculator](/standard-deviation-calculator) — enter your own values and the result updates as you type.

### What do I need to use the Standard Deviation Calculator?

Just Data set (comma or space separated). Enter those values and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. If you are unsure about a value, try a rough figure first and then refine it — the result updates instantly.
